newsitem.title: JAPAN: Palladium-Russia supply woes spur switch to nickel.
newsitem.headline: Palladium-Russia supply woes spur switch to nickel.

text.p: Japanese manufacturers of electronic components, worried about Russian palladium supplies and rising prices, are increasingly switching to cheaper metals like nickel, industry sources said on Wednesday.
"The more palladium prices rise, the more pressure we face to reduce costs, as prices of electronic components have just kept falling," a spokesman for Murata Mfg Co Ltd said.
"It is quite natural for us to forge ahead with our ongoing plans to use cheaper metals instead of palladium," he said.

Japan is the world's top consumer of palladium, and Russia is the largest supplier. In the electronics sector, palladium is used mainly in tiny components known as multi-layer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) that are used in mobile phones and a wide variety of electronic goods.
Electronics accounted for about 60 percent of Japan's total palladium demand in 1996, according to the latest report by Johnson Matthey Plc, a top palladium refiner.
Other uses of palladium, such as medical equipment, dental fillings and catalytic converters for cleaning up car exhausts, are less prone to substitution.

Concerns about Russian supplies, fuelled by the suspension of that country's exports of platinum group metals to Japan since the beginning of this year, could force manufacturers to step up the use of cheaper metals, the industry sources said.

An official with a leading Japanese electronic components manufacturer said his company could soon begin using substitute metals even in MLCCs which have a relatively small number of layers and low palladium content.

"We have nearly completed our plan to switch to cheaper metals, as we can't trust such volatile palladium prices when we're under severe pressure to cut prices of electronic components. We no longer use palladium in MLCCs with a large number of layers," said the official, who declined to be named.
"But if supply fears escalate and high prices continue, we will have to move toward nickel substitution even in MLCCs with a smaller number of layers," he said.

Precious metal industry sources pegged about 550 yen per gram as the substitution point for electronics manufacturers, which would switch to nickel and other cheaper metals once that level is breached.
While substitution requires some modifications to plant and equipment, the cost merits of using cheaper metals will accelerate the substitution plan, sources said.
The recent rally in dollar-based palladium prices, caused by a delay in Japan-Russia talks on platinum group metals for 1997, has combined with the weaker yen to push up yen-based palladium prices.

On Wednesday, spot palladium was quoted in Tokyo at 585 yen a gram, after reaching a high of 620 yen on February 28. This compares with 424 yen in late November, when world palladium prices hit a 2-1/2 year low of $114.00 an ounce.

The sources said despite rising output of MLCCs, driven by strong demand for cellular phones, palladium demand from Japan's electronic sector this year is expected to be flat or slightly lower than last year's levels due to substitution.
Industry officials estimated that TDK Corp, a major Japanese MLCC producer, now uses nickel in 90 percent of its total MLCCs and palladium in only 10 percent.
At Murata, considered more conservative in its substitution efforts, palladium accounts for about 70 percent of MLCC output while nickel accounts for the rest.
Officials from the two companies declined to give specific figures or to comment on the industry estimates.
A senior official at a major bullion house said Japan's palladium demand peaked in 1995 and worries about Russian supplies would inevitably accelerate substitution efforts.
Japan's palladium imports in 1995 hit a record high of 98.84 tonnes and slid to 77.41 tonnes in 1996, according to Finance Ministry data.
